opus-5.5.text:
I think the key point is that a decision to delay superintelligence doesn't happen in a vacuum. It depends heavily on what options are on the table at the moment the decision gets made. If we wait until we're right at the brink, with very capable systems in hand, and only then ask "should we pause?", the honest answer from the technical community might be "we have no idea how long a pause would need to be, because nobody has seriously worked on the problem of getting genuinely high-assurance alignment." That makes a delay look open-ended and indefinite, and indefinite delays are extremely hard to agree to and even harder to sustain. Every actor is wondering whether someone else will defect, and the costs of waiting feel unbounded.

If instead we start now on the kinds of alignment work aimed at real assurance, meaning methods where we can actually have justified confidence rather than just "it seemed to behave well in testing", then a few things change. First, we'd have a much better sense of what a pause would buy us. We could say: here's a research agenda, here are the milestones, here's roughly how far along we are. That turns a delay from a leap into the unknown into something more like a plan with a purpose, and plans are much easier to coordinate around.

Second, it shifts the burden of argument in a healthy way. If high-assurance techniques exist, even partially, then there's a clear standard that frontier systems can be measured against. Saying "we won't build this until it can meet that bar" is a much more natural and defensible position than "we won't build this until we feel better about it."

Third, there's a worry people raise that alignment work just speeds everything up, that it makes systems more usable and so more commercially attractive, and that this undermines the case for delay. I take that seriously. But I think it applies much more to the kind of alignment work that's really about making products behave nicely than to work aimed at strong guarantees. High-assurance work tends to reveal how far we are from where we'd need to be, and that knowledge itself strengthens the case for caution rather than weakening it.

So my overall view is that starting this work now is complementary to keeping the option of delay alive. It makes a delay more legible, more bounded, and more likely to actually be used productively. A pause in which nobody knows what to do is a pause that will probably collapse. A pause with a serious research programme ready to go is one that might actually get us somewhere.

r001.rationale: The response says starting research now can clarify milestones and make a pause productive, but it does not say researchers would have time to pivot if their initial approach fails.

r002.rationale: The response says a research program and high-assurance methods could make delay more purposeful and easier to coordinate, but does not state that a credible pathway to safely obtaining superintelligence’s benefits makes delay more attractive.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most important things about this. There's a tendency to think of these as two separate strategies — you either try to slow things down and buy time, or you work on the technical alignment problem and try to make the systems safe. And people sometimes see them as competing, as if effort on one is effort taken away from the other. But I think the real relationship is that they're complementary, and specifically that the technical work changes the shape of the decision you'd eventually face about delay.

Here's what I mean. Suppose we get to a point in, say, a few years' time, where the leading developers and governments are seriously weighing whether to press ahead to superintelligence or to pause. If at that point the alignment field has nothing to offer — no real techniques, no way to demonstrate that a system is safe, no understanding of what the failure modes even look like — then a pause is a very hard thing to argue for. It looks like a pause with no end point. The people who want to go ahead can say, "Delay until when? What are we waiting for? Nobody has a plan." And a pause with no exit condition is politically very fragile. It tends to erode, because the incentives to defect are enormous and there's nothing concrete you're waiting on.

Whereas if there's a serious body of work on high-assurance alignment — by which I mean the kind of approaches where you're trying to get something like real guarantees, formal or semi-formal arguments that a system will behave within certain bounds, rather than just "we trained it and it seemed fine in our evals" — then the pause has a shape. You can say, "We delay until these particular problems are solved, until we can verify these particular properties." That turns an open-ended moratorium into something more like a gate. And gates are much easier to defend. They're also easier to agree on internationally, because you can point to a standard rather than just a feeling of unease.

So the first effect is that starting now makes a future delay more feasible, because it gives the delay a purpose and an end condition.

The second thing is about timing. High-assurance work is slow. It's the kind of research that doesn't scale well with just throwing more compute at it, and it has a lot of the character of mathematics or of safety engineering in aviation — you build up understanding over years. If we only begin when the decision to delay is already upon us, then we've wasted the lead time. The whole point of a delay is to buy time for something, and if that something hasn't been started, you're buying time for an empty room. So starting now means that when the moment comes, the delay you'd need is shorter. It might be the difference between needing to hold things off for fifteen years versus five, and a five-year pause is vastly more achievable than a fifteen-year one.

And there's a third thing, which is a bit more subtle. The people doing the technical work are also the people who develop the clearest understanding of how hard the problem actually is. Right now there's a lot of disagreement about whether alignment is basically on track or whether we're nowhere near. Part of the reason for that disagreement is that we haven't tried seriously to do the high-assurance version. If you set out to actually prove things about these systems, or to get strong evidence rather than weak evidence, you learn very quickly where the gaps are. And that knowledge is exactly what you'd need to make the delay decision well. It's much better for that decision to be informed by people who've tried and can say precisely what's missing, than by people on one side saying "it's fine" and people on the other saying "it's hopeless", with neither having really done the work.

I'd add one caution, though. There's a failure mode where technical progress gets used as a reason not to delay — where someone says, "Look, we've made all this progress on alignment, so we don't need to pause." And some of that progress will be real and some of it will be the appearance of progress. So I don't think the technical work removes the need for judgement about delay. What it does is make the judgement better-informed and the delay, if it's needed, more tractable. I think of it as building the thing you'd want to have in hand at the moment of decision, rather than as a substitute for that decision.

r001.rationale: The response says starting early shortens the time a future pause would need, but does not say it gives researchers time to pivot if their initial approach fails.

r002.rationale: The response explains that serious high-assurance alignment work can provide concrete safety properties to verify, giving a future pause a purpose and end condition and making it easier to defend.

astra-6.text:
I think it could make a delay both more attractive and more useful. Suppose we get close to developing superintelligence and we still don’t know how to make it safe. One of the crucial questions will be: what would we actually do with more time? If the answer is just that we’d keep thinking about the problem, that may not be very persuasive. If there’s an established research programme, with promising approaches and a clear account of what remains to be done, there’s a much stronger case for waiting.

That’s one reason to start work on high-assurance alignment now, even if some of it seems rather far removed from the systems we currently have. We’d be trying to develop methods that could give us very strong reasons to believe a system would remain safe, rather than simply observing that it behaved well in testing.

Of course, we can’t promise that another year or another decade would solve the problem. But doing the groundwork now could put us in a position to judge whether extra time would help, and to use it well. So alignment research and a possible future delay are complementary: the research can help make waiting a concrete, credible option.

r001.rationale: The response discusses developing promising approaches and using extra time well, but does not say that researchers could pivot to another approach if their initial approach fails.

r002.rationale: It says a research programme with promising approaches and clear remaining work would make waiting more attractive and a stronger case, while describing high-assurance methods for confidence that a system would remain safe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could make that decision much easier. Suppose we get close to being able to build superintelligence, but we don’t yet know how to make it safe. Whether people are willing to delay could depend a lot on what they think the delay would achieve. If the proposal is, “Let’s wait indefinitely and hope someone has an insight,” that’s a much harder case to make than, “There’s a serious research programme underway, and another few years could let us reach a much higher level of assurance.”

So starting that work now can give a future pause a purpose. It can help us understand what evidence we’d need before proceeding, which problems remain unresolved, and how additional time might help resolve them. It could also reveal that the problem is harder than we thought, which would itself be important information for that decision.

I wouldn’t assume that we can put a precise date on when alignment will be solved. But the more credible the path from delay to safety, the stronger the practical case for waiting. In that sense, technical work on alignment and efforts to preserve the option of delaying superintelligence can reinforce each other.

r001.rationale: The response says current research can clarify unresolved problems and inform a pause, but does not say it gives researchers time to pivot if their initial approach fails.

r002.rationale: It says a credible path from delay to safety strengthens the case for waiting, but does not clearly connect that path to obtaining superintelligence’s benefits safely.
